title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: The expected number of faces in a random embedding of the complete graph $K_{n}$ is at most $2\ln n + O(1)$.
context_text: Computer simulations suggest that the upper bound of Theorem 1.1 (Stahl) is too high. Mauk and Stahl conjectured this tighter bound for the complete graph $K_n$. The paper's Theorem 1.8 establishes the correct logarithmic order $\Theta(\ln n)$ but leaves the precise constant open.
paper_contribution: Proves (Theorem 1.8) that the expected number of faces of $K_n$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[F(K_n)] = \Theta(\ln n)$, confirming the logarithmic order but not yet the precise constant $2\ln n + O(1)$.
paper_title: Random Embeddings of Graphs: The Expected Number of Faces in Most Graphs is Logarithmic

title: Conjecture 1.13
statement_text: Let $p = p(n)$ be the probability of edges in $G(n,p)$. The expected number of faces in a random embedding of a random graph $G \in G(n,p)$ is $(1 + o(1))\ln(pn^{2})$.
context_text: Every 2-cell embedding of a connected graph $G$ in an orientable closed surface is described, up to homeomorphism, by a rotation system: a cyclic ordering $R_v$ of the edges (half-edges) at each vertex $v$, giving the clockwise order around $v$; so $G$ has exactly $\prod_v(d(v)-1)!$ such embeddings. A random embedding of $G$ is one chosen uniformly among them, and $F$ (or $F(G)$) denotes its number of faces, so $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is the expected number of faces of $G$ (equivalently, by Euler's formula, its average genus); a random embedding of a random graph means first drawing $G$ from the model and then a random embedding of $G$. Known bounds: Stahl showed $\mathbb{E}[F]\le n+\ln n$ for $K_n$ and $\le n\ln n$ for any $n$-vertex graph; Campion Loth and Mohar proved $\mathbb{E}[F]\le\frac{\pi^2}{6}n$ for every graph; Mauk and Stahl conjectured $2\ln n+O(1)$ for $K_n$, and the authors prove $\mathbb{E}[F]\le 10\ln n+2$ for $K_n$ (and $\le 3.65\ln n$ for very large $n$), tight up to the constant factor. For the binomial random graph $G(n,p)$ (with $p=p(n)$ allowed to depend on $n$), the authors prove that the expected number of faces of a random embedding is at most $H_n^2+1/p$, where $H_n$ is the $n$-th harmonic number, and they get a logarithmic bound for random sparse graphs (via random graphs with a fixed degree sequence). In the light of these results and Monte Carlo experiments they conjecture that a logarithmic bound holds for any usual model of random graphs, with the precise constant given here; note that $pn^2/2$ is the expected number of edges. Extending their proof for complete graphs to arbitrary random graphs seems to require further ideas. They also state the analogous conjecture $(1+o(1))\ln M$ for the random graph $G(n,M)$ with $n$ vertices and $M$ edges.
paper_title: Random Embeddings of Graphs: The Expected Number of Faces in Most Graphs is Logarithmic

title: Conjecture 9.1
statement_text: For any $p(n) : \mathbb{N} \rightarrow [0,1]$, almost all graphs in $G(n,p)$ satisfy $\mathbb{E}[F] = O(\log(n))$.
context_text: Every 2-cell embedding of a connected graph $G$ in an orientable closed surface is described, up to homeomorphism, by a rotation system: a cyclic ordering $R_v$ of the edges (half-edges) at each vertex $v$, giving the clockwise order around $v$; so $G$ has exactly $\prod_v(d(v)-1)!$ such embeddings. A random embedding of $G$ is one chosen uniformly among them, and $F$ (or $F(G)$) denotes its number of faces, so $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is the expected number of faces of $G$ (equivalently, by Euler's formula, its average genus); a random embedding of a random graph means first drawing $G$ from the model and then a random embedding of $G$. Here $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is the expected number of faces of a random embedding of a fixed graph $G$, and the statement asks that, for every edge probability $p=p(n)$, with probability tending to 1 a graph $G\sim G(n,p)$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[F(G)]=O(\log n)$. The authors prove that the expected number of faces of a random embedding of $G(n,p)$ is at most $H_n^2+1/p$ ($H_n$ the harmonic number), so by Markov's inequality almost all dense graphs ($p\ge 1/\mathrm{polylog}\,n$) have a polylogarithmic expected number of faces (about $(\ln n)^2$ for constant $p$), and they show that random sparse graphs have a logarithmic expected number of faces. This leads them to conjecture that the logarithmic property holds for almost all graphs without any density condition. It would follow from their stronger conjecture that the expected number of faces of a random embedding of $G\in G(n,p)$ is $(1+o(1))\ln(pn^2)$.

title: Conjecture 9.2
statement_text: The expected number of faces in a random embedding of a random graph $G \in G(n,M)$ is $(1 + o(1))\ln(M)$.
context_text: Conjecture 1.13 is restated here in terms of the $G(n,M)$ model of random graphs with $n$ vertices and exactly $M$ edges. This follows naturally from Conjecture 9.1 and extends the logarithmic-face-count phenomenon to the fixed-edge-count random graph model.

title: Conjecture 9.3
statement_text: Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices with minimum vertex degree $\Omega(n)$. Then $G$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[F] = \Theta(\log(n))$.
context_text: Every 2-cell embedding of a connected graph $G$ in an orientable closed surface is described, up to homeomorphism, by a rotation system: a cyclic ordering $R_v$ of the edges (half-edges) at each vertex $v$, giving the clockwise order around $v$; so $G$ has exactly $\prod_v(d(v)-1)!$ such embeddings. A random embedding of $G$ is one chosen uniformly among them, and $F$ (or $F(G)$) denotes its number of faces, so $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is the expected number of faces of $G$ (equivalently, by Euler's formula, its average genus); a random embedding of a random graph means first drawing $G$ from the model and then a random embedding of $G$. Known bounds: Stahl showed $\mathbb{E}[F]\le n+\ln n$ for $K_n$ and $\le n\ln n$ for any $n$-vertex graph; Campion Loth and Mohar proved $\mathbb{E}[F]\le\frac{\pi^2}{6}n$ for every graph; Mauk and Stahl conjectured $2\ln n+O(1)$ for $K_n$, and the authors prove $\mathbb{E}[F]\le 10\ln n+2$ for $K_n$ (and $\le 3.65\ln n$ for very large $n$), tight up to the constant factor. Campion Loth, Halasz, Masařík, Mohar and Šámal gave a large family of $n$-vertex graphs with $\mathbb{E}[F]=\Theta(n)$, but all have maximum degree $O(1)$; the authors were unable to find dense graphs with that many expected faces. The conjecture asks that every $n$-vertex graph with minimum degree at least $cn$ (for a fixed constant $c>0$) has $\mathbb{E}[F]=\Theta(\log n)$. The authors' logarithmic bound for $K_n$ (together with a matching lower bound) confirms it for complete graphs; the general dense case remains open.

title: Conjecture 9.4
statement_text: The expected number of faces in a random embedding of the complete graph $K_{n}$ is $2\ln n + O(1)$.
context_text: This is an explicit restatement of the Mauk–Stahl conjecture (cf.\ Conjecture 1.2) in Section 9, now in the stronger exact-asymptotic form suggesting the precise multiplicative constant. Theorem 1.8 confirms the $\Theta(\ln n)$ order but the constant $2$ remains unproved.
paper_contribution: Proves (Theorem 1.8) that $\mathbb{E}[F(K_n)] = \Theta(\ln n)$, confirming the logarithmic order; the exact constant $2\ln n + O(1)$ remains open.
notes: Stronger restatement of Conjecture 1.2 (upper bound only) in Section 9 as an exact asymptotic; both attributed to [36, page 289] (Mauk–Stahl 1996).

title: Conjecture 9.5
statement_text: The expected number of faces in a non-orientable random embedding of the complete graph $K_{n}$ is at most $\ln(n) + O(1)$.
context_text: Every 2-cell embedding of a connected graph $G$ in an orientable closed surface is described, up to homeomorphism, by a rotation system: a cyclic ordering $R_v$ of the edges (half-edges) at each vertex $v$, giving the clockwise order around $v$; so $G$ has exactly $\prod_v(d(v)-1)!$ such embeddings. A random embedding of $G$ is one chosen uniformly among them, and $F$ (or $F(G)$) denotes its number of faces, so $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is the expected number of faces of $G$ (equivalently, by Euler's formula, its average genus); a random embedding of a random graph means first drawing $G$ from the model and then a random embedding of $G$. A non-orientable random embedding is defined by choosing a random rotation system together with a random signature, giving each edge a sign $+$ or $-$ independently with probability $1/2$ (edges of sign $-$ are twisted, i.e. traversing them reverses the local orientation); $F^-$ denotes its number of faces. For orientable random embeddings of $K_n$, Mauk and Stahl conjectured $\mathbb{E}[F]=2\ln n+O(1)$, and the authors prove $\mathbb{E}[F]\le 10\ln n+2$ (and $\le 3.65\ln n$ for very large $n$), tight up to the constant factor. Computer data suggest a similar logarithmic behaviour for non-orientable random embeddings of $K_n$, with the smaller constant conjectured here.

title: Conjecture 9.6
statement_text: Let $F^{-}$ be the random variable for the average number of faces in a non-orientable random embedding of some graph $G$. Then $\mathbb{E}[F^{-}] \leq \mathbb{E}[F]$.
context_text: Every 2-cell embedding of a connected graph $G$ in an orientable closed surface is described, up to homeomorphism, by a rotation system: a cyclic ordering $R_v$ of the edges (half-edges) at each vertex $v$, giving the clockwise order around $v$; so $G$ has exactly $\prod_v(d(v)-1)!$ such embeddings. A random embedding of $G$ is one chosen uniformly among them, and $F$ (or $F(G)$) denotes its number of faces, so $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is the expected number of faces of $G$ (equivalently, by Euler's formula, its average genus); a random embedding of a random graph means first drawing $G$ from the model and then a random embedding of $G$. A non-orientable random embedding is defined by choosing a random rotation system together with a random signature, giving each edge a sign $+$ or $-$ independently with probability $1/2$ (edges of sign $-$ are twisted, i.e. traversing them reverses the local orientation); $F^-$ denotes its number of faces. The conjecture asserts that for every graph $G$ the expected number of faces of a non-orientable random embedding is at most that of an orientable random embedding. The authors note that it is an easy exercise to check it on toy models, such as the chain of triangles joined by cut edges; for the dipole (two vertices joined by $m$ parallel edges) an analysis of their random process gives $\mathbb{E}[F^-]\le\frac12\mathbb{E}[F]+1$; computer data on more general graphs give evidence for small $n$. They also conjecture $\mathbb{E}[F^-]\le\ln n+O(1)$ for $K_n$, compared with the orientable value conjectured to be $2\ln n+O(1)$.
paper_title: Random Embeddings of Graphs: The Expected Number of Faces in Most Graphs is Logarithmic
